Gastrointestinal physiology.contentEvidence: Digestion and absorption, bile and pancreatic secretions, gastrointestinal hormones, lipid transport, villi, peristalsis, gastrin and exercise-related splanchnic responses.

questions.text: Which site is the principal location for digestion and absorption of most dietary nutrients?
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 23 (The Digestive System), describes the small intestine as the major site of chemical digestion and nutrient absorption.

questions.text: Bile salts assist fat digestion primarily by:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 23, explains that bile salts emulsify fats, increasing the surface area available to lipase.

questions.text: When acidic chyme enters the duodenum, secretin primarily stimulates the pancreas to release:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 23, describes secretin release in response to duodenal acid and its stimulation of pancreatic bicarbonate secretion.

questions.text: Cholecystokinin released after a fatty meal helps digestion mainly by causing:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 23, identifies cholecystokinin as a response to fats and proteins that promotes gallbladder contraction and pancreatic secretion.

questions.text: Most absorbed long-chain dietary lipids initially enter the circulation through the:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 23, explains that larger lipid products are packaged into chylomicrons and enter intestinal lacteals before reaching the blood.

questions.text: Villi and microvilli increase intestinal absorption primarily by:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 23, describes villi and microvilli as adaptations that greatly increase the absorptive surface of the small intestine.

questions.text: Peristalsis is best described as:
questions.correctOption: Coordinated smooth-muscle waves that propel gastrointestinal contents
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 23, describes peristalsis as coordinated muscular contractions that move gastrointestinal contents along the tract.

questions.text: Gastrin primarily promotes which gastrointestinal response?
questions.correctOption: Gastric acid secretion and gastric motility
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 23, describes gastrin as a hormone that supports gastric secretion and motility.

questions.text: During prolonged exercise, reduced splanchnic blood flow can contribute to gastrointestinal symptoms because:
questions.correctOption: Blood is redirected away from the gut
questions.explanation: Physiology of Sport and Exercise, Kenney, Wilmore and Costill, 5th edition, sections on exercise blood-flow redistribution and gastrointestinal responses, describes reduced gut perfusion and exercise stress as contributors to gastrointestinal symptoms.

questions.text: A person with impaired pancreatic bicarbonate secretion would have the greatest difficulty:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 23, explains the role of pancreatic bicarbonate in neutralising acidic chyme in the duodenum.

Reproductive physiology.contentEvidence: Hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal signalling, Leydig and Sertoli cell function, ovulation, corpus luteum, progesterone, inhibin, follicular oestrogen and low-energy-availability effects.

questions.text: Which hypothalamic hormone initiates reproductive-axis signalling by stimulating pituitary gonadotropin release?
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 27 (The Reproductive System), describes hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone as the signal that regulates pituitary FSH and LH secretion.

questions.text: Luteinising hormone acts on Leydig cells primarily to stimulate:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 27, explains that LH stimulates testosterone production by the interstitial (Leydig) cells of the testes.

questions.text: Follicle-stimulating hormone supports male reproductive function mainly by acting on:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 27, describes FSH action on Sertoli cells and its role in supporting spermatogenesis.

questions.text: The mid-cycle surge of which hormone triggers ovulation?
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 27, identifies the mid-cycle LH surge as the endocrine trigger for ovulation.

questions.text: After ovulation, the corpus luteum primarily secretes:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 27, describes the corpus luteum as a source of progesterone during the luteal phase.

questions.text: Progesterone during the luteal phase helps to:
questions.correctOption: Maintain a secretory endometrium for implantation
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 27, explains progesterone effects on the endometrium during the luteal phase and preparation for implantation.

questions.text: Inhibin provides negative feedback on pituitary secretion mainly by reducing:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 27, describes inhibin feedback as selectively reducing FSH secretion.

questions.text: During the follicular phase, rising oestrogen from developing ovarian follicles helps to:
questions.correctOption: Promote proliferative growth of the endometrium
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 27, describes follicular oestrogen production and its proliferative effects on the uterine lining.

questions.text: Which event is most directly associated with the follicular phase of the ovarian cycle?
questions.correctOption: Development and maturation of an ovarian follicle
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 27, describes follicular development as the defining ovarian event of the follicular phase.

questions.text: Low energy availability in an athlete can impair reproductive function partly by reducing:
questions.explanation: IOC consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport: 2023 update, reproductive-health sections, describes low energy availability as capable of disrupting hypothalamic reproductive signalling and menstrual function.

Special-senses physiology.contentEvidence: Rods, semicircular canals, organ of Corti, fovea, vestibulo-ocular reflex, accommodation, optic-chiasm fibre crossing, phototransduction, otolith organs and middle-ear ossicles.

questions.text: Which retinal photoreceptors are most important for vision in dim light?
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 17 (The Special Senses), describes rods as highly sensitive photoreceptors used especially in low-light vision.

questions.text: The semicircular canals primarily detect:
questions.correctOption: Angular or rotational acceleration of the head
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 17, describes the semicircular canals as receptors for rotational movement and angular acceleration.

questions.text: The organ of Corti is located in the:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 17, locates the organ of Corti in the cochlea, where auditory transduction occurs.

questions.text: The fovea centralis provides the highest visual acuity because it contains a high concentration of:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 17, describes the fovea as the retinal region with the greatest cone density and visual acuity.

questions.text: The vestibulo-ocular reflex helps an athlete maintain a stable visual target when the head:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 17, explains vestibular contributions to reflex eye movements that stabilise gaze during head movement.

questions.text: For a near object, accommodation of the eye requires the lens to become:
questions.correctOption: Becomes rounder as ciliary tension falls
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 17, describes near accommodation as ciliary-muscle contraction that allows the lens to become more rounded.

questions.text: At the optic chiasm, which fibres cross to the opposite side?
questions.correctOption: Nasal retinal fibres from each eye
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 17, describes crossing of nasal retinal fibres at the optic chiasm.

questions.text: In phototransduction, light exposure normally causes a photoreceptor membrane to:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 17, explains that light reduces cyclic GMP, closes cation channels and hyperpolarises photoreceptors.

questions.text: The utricle and saccule are most involved in sensing:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 17, describes the utricle and saccule as otolith organs that detect linear acceleration and head position.

questions.text: The middle-ear ossicles primarily function to:
questions.explanation: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 17, describes the malleus, incus and stapes as transmitting and amplifying tympanic-membrane vibrations to the inner ear.

Yoga basics.officialSyllabusArea: Exercise Therapy and Rehabilitation — massage therapy and yoga basics
Yoga basics.contentEvidence: Asana, pranayama, mind-body practice, safe instruction, non-forceful progression, symptom monitoring, balance, adjunctive use and controlled breathing.

questions.text: In basic yoga terminology, an asana is a:
questions.explanation: NCCIH, Yoga: Effectiveness and Safety, “What is yoga,” identifies asana as the physical-posture component of yoga practice.

questions.text: Pranayama refers most directly to the practice of:
questions.explanation: NCCIH, Yoga: Effectiveness and Safety, “What is yoga,” identifies pranayama as breathing practices used within yoga.

questions.text: Which introductory yoga instruction is most consistent with safe practice?
questions.explanation: NCCIH, Yoga: Effectiveness and Safety, “What are the risks,” recommends qualified instruction and cautions against forceful or extreme practice.

questions.text: An athlete with acute knee pain feels discomfort in a deep yoga squat. The most appropriate response is to:
questions.correctOption: Modify or stop the posture and reassess the knee
questions.explanation: NCCIH, Yoga: Effectiveness and Safety, advises adapting practice and avoiding forceful techniques; a painful posture should be modified and clinically reassessed.

questions.text: A yoga session that combines postures with deliberate breathing and attention is best described as:
questions.explanation: NCCIH, Yoga: Effectiveness and Safety, describes yoga as a practice combining physical postures, breathing techniques and meditation or attention.

questions.text: For an athlete using yoga to supplement rehabilitation, the safest progression is generally to:
questions.explanation: NCCIH, Yoga: Effectiveness and Safety, supports safe instruction and avoidance of extreme techniques; progression should therefore be gradual and symptom-aware.

questions.text: Which outcome is most plausibly targeted by a controlled yoga balance posture?
questions.explanation: Effect of yoga on selected performance metrics and mental health of track and field athletes: A systematic review, Singh et al., 2025, reports balance and flexibility as performance-related outcomes studied in yoga interventions.

questions.text: An athlete reports that a yoga session produces a mild, short-lived stretch sensation without worsening symptoms the next day. The best interpretation is:
questions.explanation: NCCIH, Yoga: Effectiveness and Safety, supports safe practice within individual tolerance; a favourable response does not remove the need for graded monitoring.

questions.text: Which statement about yoga and sports performance is most defensible?
questions.correctOption: Yoga may help as an adjunct; effects vary
questions.explanation: Effect of yoga on selected performance metrics and mental health of track and field athletes: A systematic review, Singh et al., 2025, supports cautious interpretation of yoga as an adjunct rather than a universal replacement or guarantee.

questions.text: During a basic yoga session, diaphragmatic breathing is most appropriately used to:
questions.explanation: NCCIH, Yoga: Effectiveness and Safety, describes breathing practice as a component of yoga and recommends safe, non-forceful participation; breathing should support controlled movement rather than strain.

Body-composition assessment and anthropo.contentEvidence: BMI formula and calculation, BMI limitations, skinfolds, standardisation, waist circumference, body-mass interpretation, hydration effects, measurement error and contextual interpretation.

questions.text: Body mass index is calculated as:
questions.correctOption: Body mass in kilograms divided by height in metres squared
questions.explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, defines BMI as body mass in kilograms divided by height in metres squared.

questions.text: An athlete weighs 81 kg and is 1.80 m tall. The approximate BMI is:
questions.explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, supports the BMI calculation: 81 ÷ 1.80² is approximately 25.0 kg/m².

questions.text: A major limitation of BMI when used with a muscular athlete is that it:
questions.correctOption: Cannot distinguish fat mass from lean mass
questions.explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, cautions that BMI does not distinguish fat mass from fat-free mass.

questions.text: Skinfold assessment primarily measures:
questions.explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, describes skinfolds as measures of subcutaneous fat used in prediction equations for body composition.

questions.text: For repeated skinfold measurements to be more interpretable, the assessor should:
questions.correctOption: Use a consistent protocol, sites and trained technique
questions.explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, emphasises standardised sites, technique and assessor procedures for reliable repeated measures.

questions.text: Which measurement is a direct anthropometric circumference measure commonly used in body-composition interpretation?
questions.explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, includes circumference measures such as waist circumference within anthropometric assessment.

questions.text: An athlete loses 2 kg over a training block. Which conclusion is most defensible without further assessment?
questions.correctOption: The change may include fluid and tissue
questions.explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, supports interpreting body-mass change with additional measures because mass alone cannot identify the tissues or fluid responsible.

questions.text: A dehydrated athlete shows a lower body mass before testing. The body-composition result should be interpreted with caution because:
questions.correctOption: Hydration can alter mass and estimates
questions.explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, supports standardised testing and cautions that hydration status affects body-mass interpretation and some methods.

questions.text: A small change in a skinfold measurement that is within the method’s expected measurement error should be:
questions.correctOption: Interpret it cautiously as possible change
questions.explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, supports considering measurement error and standardisation before interpreting small changes in skinfold-derived estimates.

questions.text: A BMI of 27 kg/m² in an adult athlete should initially be regarded as:
questions.correctOption: A screening value that needs context
questions.explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, uses BMI as a screening measure and notes that interpretation requires context, especially in muscular athletes.
